tldr: By introducing gripper-centric "contact topologies" that do not depend on object shapes, the authors propose "CoToGrasp," a dexterous grasp planner for multi-fingered hands that generates intended grasp styles (such as precision pinches or powerful power grasps) with high fidelity without using any object meshes during training.
hero_caption: Overall concept of CoToGrasp. Given only a desired contact topology (precision grasp, tool use, power grasp, etc.) and an unseen object geometry, it synthesizes stable grasping poses satisfying the target function via a hand-specific canonical workspace, completely without training on object meshes.
overview:
Recent research on multi-fingered robot grasping has primarily optimized for "physical stability"—whether an object can be held without dropping. Consequently, planners suffer from mode collapse (loss of diversity), overwhelmingly generating easy-to-stabilize "power grasps" where the whole palm encloses the object, while struggling severely with "functional grasps" like fingertip precision pinches or specialized grasps for tool use. Furthermore, conditioning on grasp taxonomies has traditionally required prohibitively expensive datasets manually annotated across vast numbers of objects.

The authors fundamentally inverted this mindset. Instead of searching for "where to touch on the object," they focused on gripper-centric contact topologies: "which parts of the hand should contact the object." By defining a feature-based canonical workspace fixed to the hand's reference frame, the model learns solely the relationship between the hand's own geometry and contact masks during training. In other words, they adopted an "object-agnostic" approach that trains the model completely without object data.

At inference time, unseen object point clouds are simply projected into this unified workspace, where a Transformer and a CVAE (Conditional Variational Autoencoder) instantly predict contact patches satisfying the specified contact topology. Furthermore, by inserting geometric label consistency checks and physical force-closure assessments before joint angle optimization, failing poses are pruned efficiently. Extensive evaluations on the large-scale DexGraspNet dataset and a physical robot platform demonstrate superior grasp success rates and overwhelmingly high topological fidelity over existing methods.
contributions: Formulated an object-agnostic generative framework that learns contact capabilities solely from the hand's own geometry without requiring any object models during training.
Decoupled arbitrary object geometries from semantic functional grasping intent by projecting local geometric features via a palm-centric canonical workspace.
Combined a Transformer self-attention mechanism, which prevents the dilution of topological instructions, with a CVAE to accurately predict probabilistic grasp contact distributions.
Established an asymmetric Tversky index-based evaluation metric and an entropy metric to rigorously assess how faithfully generated grasps adhere to specified topologies.

sections.heading: Why is stable grasping alone not enough?
sections.summary: Multi-fingered hands are inherently capable of diverse contact patterns, such as delicate fingertip manipulation and tool holding. However, because conventional planners focus solely on physical stability, they suffer from a severe bias toward crude palm-enclosing grasps. This paper proposes CoToGrasp, a novel method that conditions on "contact topologies" rooted in human grasp taxonomy to synthesize grasps as an intrinsic hand capability without using object data.
sections.details:
In an era where humanoid robots collaborate with high-level reasoning engines like Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform complex tasks, grasping can no longer just solve "whether an object can be held geometrically without dropping." Downstream operations such as object reorientation, tool insertion, and finger gaiting critically require controllable multi-point contacts powered by high-DoF hands.

However, current data-driven grasp planners have a structural flaw. Because their objective functions optimize solely for force equilibrium (force closure) or energetic stability, planners inevitably collapse into generating the simplest, most stable "power grasps." As a result, when downstream tasks demand a specific precision pinch grasp, robots are forced into extremely inefficient searches, generating and discarding hundreds or thousands of unsuitable candidates.

To overcome this challenge, the authors turned to the grasp taxonomy by Gonzalez et al. This taxonomy classifies grasps into 21 types based purely on "which surfaces of the hand are actively in contact," regardless of object shape. Furthermore, recognizing that pairing object geometries one-to-one with grasp poses in training datasets hinders generalization to unseen objects, they adopted an "object-agnostic" paradigm that learns the contact capability of the hand itself without using any objects.

The proposed method, "CoToGrasp," uses a canonical workspace fixed to the hand coordinate frame as a bridge, aggregating local features and generating probabilistic contact masks via a Transformer and a CVAE. Both simulations and physical robot experiments demonstrate that this dramatically resolves conventional bias.

sections.heading: Limitations of existing methods and the new object-agnostic paradigm
sections.summary: Conventional grasp synthesis models rely on analytical stability datasets and easily suffer from mode collapse toward power grasps. Meanwhile, prior taxonomy-guided works suffer from tightly coupling object meshes with joint angles. CoToGrasp leverages contact duality for object-agnostic learning, entirely eliminating the need for massive, expensive object-annotated datasets.
sections.details:
Related work can be organized into three main lines:

- Learning-based grasp planners: Approaches directly predicting joint angles or learning intermediate representations (such as contact maps) are popular. However, because they rely on synthetic datasets solving solely for mechanical stability, whole-palm-enclosing grasps dominate, failing to unlock the true dexterity of multi-fingered hands. They also tend to overfit to specific objects and generalize poorly to novel shapes. In contrast, object-agnostic approaches that learn contacts within the hand's domain (such as GOAG) have begun to show superior generalization.

- Human grasp taxonomies and task-oriented grasping: Classic comprehensive grasp taxonomies include those by Cutkosky and Feix et al., while Gonzalez et al. proposed a 21-class taxonomy focused on active contact surfaces. Recently, vision-language models (VLMs) have been explored to guide grasp selection, but approaches retargeting human demonstrations directly to robot hands suffer from high reliance on demonstration data.

- Taxonomy-conditioned grasp synthesis: Recent works like Dexonomy and OmniDexVLG attempt to synthesize grasp poses conditioned on taxonomy. However, these methods learn from datasets of "precomputed joint angle combinations for specific object meshes." If an unseen object shape deviates even slightly from that joint template, the optimization fails or collapses into an incorrect grasp type.

The decisive difference in CoToGrasp is that it defines taxonomy as "semantic contact masks" rather than rigid joint angles and trains without objects. This completely breaks the dependency on expensive annotated datasets.

sections.heading: How the canonical workspace and Transformer predict contacts
sections.summary: Leveraging the symmetric relationship (duality) of contact between hand and object, this method projects local geometric features of objects into a palm-centric canonical workspace. A Transformer with self-attention and a CVAE generate contact regions satisfying the specified topology, and only candidates passing geometric and physical checks are converted into final joint angles via energy optimization.
sections.details:
The CoToGrasp pipeline is clearly divided into two phases: training and inference/synthesis.

3.1 Gripper-Centric Contact Topology
Active contact points on the hand surface ($N_H=2048$ points) are termed the handprint ${\cal H}$. Based on the taxonomy by Gonzalez et al., the hand surface is partitioned into 22 zones to define 21 contact topology templates ${\cal A}_m$. These serve as semantic masks indicating "which zones should be in contact."

3.2 Geometric Transfer via Canonical Workspace Learning
Contact is a "dual" relationship between hand and object. Instead of searching over unbounded object surfaces with infinite shape variations, the problem is inverted into the bounded space of the hand surface, which has fixed degrees of freedom and geometry. A "Canonical Workspace (${\cal W}$)" is placed with its origin fixed to the palm in the hand coordinate frame. Geometric features extracted by DGCNN are aggregated into representative workspace points using k-nearest neighbors (kNN) based on a normal-aligned distance metric (${\cal D}_{\text{aligned}}$). The domain gap is bridged by projecting the hand's own geometry during training and an inverted-normal point cloud of the target object during inference.

3.3 Contact Template Learning with Self-Attention
For the projected spatial tokens, the embedding of the specified topology is directly concatenated to each point (persistent hard conditioning), and a Transformer encoder captures global spatial relationships across points. Subsequently, features are compressed via a Set Transformer, and a CVAE (Conditional Variational Autoencoder) outputs a probabilistic contact mask $\hat{\Lambda}_m$.

3.4 Cascaded Validation and Grasp Synthesis
At inference time, after transforming the object into hand space and predicting contact masks, two stages of fast checks are executed before running heavy physical optimization:
- Label consistency check: Computes the XOR between the predicted mask and target template, immediately discarding degenerate poses exceeding tolerance (up to 1 zone missing or redundant).
- Fast force-closure verification: Rapidly constructs the Grasp Wrench Space from centroids of active regions to verify theoretical equilibrium. If infeasible, the latent variable $z$ is resampled (up to 20 times).
Finally, optimal joint angles $Q^*$ are determined by minimizing an energy function combining terms for attraction to target contact points, interpenetration avoidance, self-collision avoidance, joint limits, and a "repulsion term ($E_{\text{rep}}$) keeping non-participating fingers and palm at least 5 mm away from the object."

The lower row depicts the inference phase, where an unseen object point cloud is fed in, and contact predictions are passed through consistency and force-closure checks before energy optimization yields final joint angles.

sections.heading: Breaking mode collapse! Thorough validation from precision pinch to physical hardware
sections.summary: Compared against taxonomy-free baselines and the state-of-the-art Dexonomy in simulation, CoToGrasp eliminated the bias toward power grasps, achieving both high semantic fidelity (TC) and fast generation (0.11 s per grasp). Furthermore, deploying it on a physical 4-fingered robot hand (Allegro Hand) confirmed stable, diverse grasps on novel objects.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted using the Shadow Hand (simulation) and the 4-fingered Allegro Hand (physical robot).

4.1 Evaluation Setup and Novel Metrics
To measure grasp fidelity, actual contact regions of synthesized grasps were automatically extracted, and a new metric, "Topology Compliance (TC)," based on an asymmetric Tversky index was introduced to strictly penalize redundant contacts (clumsy enclosing). Additionally, "Semantic Entropy ($\textbf{H}_{TC}$)" was defined to measure diversity in the generation distribution (values closer to 1 indicate balanced diversity, while 0 indicates bias and collapse into a single type).

4.2 Comparison with Taxonomy-Free Baselines
CoToGrasp was compared against DFC, GenDexGrasp, DRO-Grasp, and GOAG on the MultiDex dataset. While existing methods exhibited superficially high Success Rates (SR) by overwhelmingly generating enclosing grasps (such as M21), their semantic entropy $\textbf{H}_{TC}$ remained poor (0.60 to 0.74). In contrast, CoToGrasp did not evade challenging conditions like fingertip pinch grasps, achieving the highest $\textbf{H}_{TC}$ (0.83). Moreover, its generation time was 0.11 s per grasp, recording by far the fastest speed among all baselines.

4.3 Head-to-Head Comparison with Taxonomy-Guided Dexonomy
In evaluations across 1,126 unseen objects from DexGraspNet, CoToGrasp outperformed Dexonomy in both grasp success rate and Topology Compliance (TC: 17.18% vs. 14.28%). Notably, on challenging fingertip precision grasps (M2), CoToGrasp achieved 30.3% compared to Dexonomy's 10.5%. When facing complex geometries, Dexonomy tended to ignore instructions and regress into enclosing grasps (mode collapse) to boost superficial success rates. CoToGrasp prunes unsuitable candidates via prior validation, thereby realizing genuine functional grasping.

4.4 Physical Robot Validation
Using a physical setup comprising a UR10 arm and an Allegro Hand, grasping tests were conducted on diverse YCB dataset objects. In a real environment with cameras and markers, the system demonstrated stable lifting across objects like mustard bottles, balls, and drills by properly utilizing fingertips or palms according to specified topologies (M1–M18).

captions.F4: Comparison of contact topology generation distributions against taxonomy-free planners. Existing methods exhibit an extreme bias toward enclosing power grasps (M15 and M21, highlighted in red boxes), whereas CoToGrasp (red bars) maintains a remarkably uniform distribution, including precision grasps.
captions.F5: Physical validation using a UR10 robot arm and an Allegro Hand. It shows that diverse grasping poses conditioned on specified contact topologies (M1–M18) can be physically executed to stably grasp and lift various everyday objects from the YCB dataset.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Unleashing the true potential of dexterous robot hands
sections.summary: By completely decoupling functional grasp intent from object geometry, CoToGrasp overcomes the inherent bias toward power grasps that plagued prior planners. It demonstrates that multi-fingered grasps faithfully reproducing specified contact topologies on novel objects can be generated instantaneously, even when trained entirely without object datasets.
sections.details:
The core breakthrough of this work lies in embedding the functional semantics of "how to grasp an object" as an intrinsic geometric and kinematic capability of the robot hand itself, fully disentangled from object shape. This allows zero-shot adaptation to novel object shapes without curating massive annotated object mesh datasets.

Furthermore, the label consistency check and force-closure verification integrated into the inference pipeline filter out geometrically implausible candidates early on, significantly enhancing optimization convergence and reliability. Physical experiments also confirmed that contact topologies derived in simulation transfer effectively to real multi-fingered hardware. CoToGrasp holds great promise as a practical low-level grasp generator capable of responding immediately when high-level planners, such as LLMs, issue commands like "pinch here to use this tool."

sections.heading: Appendix: Network design details and real-robot control hurdles
sections.summary: The appendix details local feature aggregation in the canonical workspace, quantitative evidence of feature alignment for bridging domain shift, robustness against complex non-convex shapes, and hardware-specific limitations and future challenges arising from position control.
sections.details:
Several important technical details provide deeper insight into the paper:

- Handprint Discretization and Taxonomy Porting: Active contact surfaces are filtered by computing inner products with the hand approach direction (palm normal) and discretized into $N_H=2048$ points. For the 4-fingered Allegro Hand, the framework is smoothly ported simply by excluding the 5-finger-dependent template (${\cal A}_6$) (Fig. F7).

- Local Feature Extraction and Canonical Projection Nuances: Because global shape descriptors wash out fine surface curvatures and normals, a dynamic graph CNN (DGCNN) is employed to preserve local features. Furthermore, kNN projection into the workspace deliberately avoids normalization (dividing by the sum of weights), allowing features to naturally decay to zero with distance and preventing the hallucination of object features in empty space.

- Cross-Domain Feature Alignment: Quantifying the domain gap between training (hand points) and inference (object points) revealed that cosine similarity, which was initially low at 0.35 right after DGCNN, surged to 0.61 following kNN canonical projection and further reached 0.66 after passing through Transformer self-attention.

- Robustness to Shape Complexity (Non-Convexity): In an analysis using object convex hull volume ratios (Table 7) on highly complex shapes with severe concavities, Dexonomy's success rate dropped to 37.42%, whereas CoToGrasp maintained 58.72%. Furthermore, its Topology Compliance (TC) actually increased (19.17%), demonstrating the advantage of grounding contacts in local features.

- Limitations and Challenges in Hardware Control: When executing precision grasps on real hardware using standard trajectory interpolation under position control, fingertips making premature contact were observed to push the object away, causing deviations from target contact positions. The authors conclude that integrating hybrid position/force control or tactile feedback policies will be essential moving forward.

captions.F7: Anatomical contact zone partition maps for the 5-fingered Shadow Hand (left) and 4-fingered Allegro Hand (right). This shows how hands with different finger counts can be adapted to a common topology template framework.

takeaways: Inverting the problem to predict hand contact regions within a fixed workspace rather than finding object contact points enables object-agnostic learning without object meshes.
Combining global Transformer attention with energy optimization containing a repulsion term achieves strict precision grasping while preventing unintended finger contacts.

True dexterity and diversity in multi-fingered grasping cannot be evaluated by simple Success Rate (SR) alone; metrics like asymmetric Tversky evaluation (TC) and entropy that penalize unintended contacts are necessary.
limitations: When executed under pure position control (e.g., MoveIt) on physical hardware, slight timing differences in fingertip contacts push the object, causing deviations from the target contact topology (integration with force control or tactile feedback is not yet implemented).
The 6-DoF hand approach pose relies on heuristics or an external planner, meaning end-to-end approach trajectory planning is not included.

Due to the strict definition of Topology Compliance (TC), slight, physically unavoidable touches of adjacent phalanges against the object caused by finger length limits are strictly penalized as failures, representing an overly stringent aspect of the evaluation.
